opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I think this is one of the most underappreciated forces in history, and it's central to how I think about technology and governance.

The basic idea goes back to people like Charles Tilly, who argued that "war made the state, and the state made war." In early modern Europe, the polities that survived were the ones that could mobilize resources for war: raising taxes, building bureaucracies, fielding large standing armies. Over time, that selection pressure shaped what states looked like internally. You got centralized administration, professional civil services, national identities, and eventually mass education, partly because a literate, healthy, loyal population made better soldiers and workers.

What I find striking is how that pressure carried into the modern era with industrialization. Once war became a contest of whole economies, states needed the cooperation of very large parts of the population. You needed factory workers, engineers, and mass conscript armies. Many scholars argue this helped drive the expansion of the franchise and the welfare state. If you're asking millions of people to fight and work for the nation, they gain bargaining power, and elites have strong incentives to grant them political inclusion. So in a sense, the military-economic logic of the 19th and 20th centuries was fairly friendly to broad-based, participatory politics.

The thing I worry about, and the reason this matters for AI, is that this alignment isn't guaranteed. It was contingent on a particular technological situation where power depended on mass human labor and mass human soldiers. If advanced AI and automation reduce how much states need broad populations to generate wealth and military strength, the incentives that historically pushed toward inclusion could weaken. You might see something more like the resource curse: governments that rely on oil rents rather than taxing their citizens often become less accountable, because they don't need the population's cooperation.

So when I look at military competition today, I see two things happening. First, there's the familiar pressure: great powers racing to adopt powerful technologies because falling behind feels existentially risky. That can push states to prioritize speed and capability over safety, deliberation, and civil liberties. Second, and more subtly, the content of what wins that competition may be shifting in ways that change the domestic bargain between governments and citizens.

None of this is destiny. Technological and competitive pressures shape the landscape, but institutions, norms, and international agreements can steer within it. To me, the lesson is that if we care about preserving democratic, accountable governance, we can't assume it will be selected for automatically. We have to think deliberately about how to structure competition, and where possible cooperation, so that the kinds of societies we want remain competitive and stable in a world with very powerful AI.

r001.rationale: The response links military competition to domestic changes such as broader franchise and welfare, but attributes those changes to the need for mass participation. It separately says fear of falling behind can lead states to prioritize speed and capability; it does not clearly connect claims of losing strategic position against an adversary to domestic reform.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I've thought about a lot, and I think the historical pattern is actually quite striking once you look for it. There's this long tradition in political science and sociology — Charles Tilly, Otto Hintze, more recently people like Herbst — of arguing that the modern state was in many ways forged by war. The need to raise armies, to finance them, to extract resources from the population: that's what built bureaucracies, tax systems, standing administrations. Tilly's famous line is "war made the state, and the state made war."

But what I find most interesting for thinking about the modern era is the second-order effect, which is what military competition does to the relationship between rulers and the ruled. If the way you win wars depends on mass mobilization — on getting large numbers of ordinary people to fight and to pay — then rulers have to bargain with those people. You see this with the expansion of the franchise in the 19th and early 20th centuries, with the growth of the welfare state, with the development of mass education. A lot of that is partly downstream of military necessity. If you need millions of literate, healthy, loyal soldiers, you end up investing in your population and giving them a political stake. So in that era, military competition was, perhaps counterintuitively, a democratizing force in some respects.

The worry I have about the present and the near future is that this relationship can flip. The key variable is what the sources of military power actually are. If military power increasingly comes from capital-intensive, technologically sophisticated systems — advanced AI, autonomous weapons, sophisticated surveillance and cyber capabilities — rather than from mass armies, then the state no longer needs its population in the same way. It doesn't need to bargain with them. And in fact, it might increasingly view the population less as a resource and more as a potential source of instability to be managed.

So you can imagine a trajectory where military competition between great powers pushes states toward concentrating power in whoever controls the relevant technologies, toward secrecy and national-security exceptions to normal democratic oversight, toward prioritizing speed over deliberation. And at the same time, the very technologies that confer military advantage — pervasive surveillance, automated enforcement — are also exactly the tools you'd want if you wanted to lock in a particular political order. That's a dangerous combination.

I don't want to be deterministic about this. Domestic institutions, political culture, the choices leaders make — these all matter enormously, and there are plenty of historical cases where the pressures I'm describing were resisted. But I do think the default pressures from intense military competition in a world of transformative technology point in a concerning direction, and that's one of the reasons I care so much about whether we can find ways to dampen that competition — through arms control, through building trust and verification mechanisms, through shared norms — rather than just assuming that the domestic politics will take care of themselves.

r001.rationale: The response links military competition and wartime needs to reforms such as expanding the franchise, welfare, and education. It does not state that claims of risking a loss of strategic position against an adversary motivate those reforms.

astra-6.text:
I think one useful starting point is that military competition changes what states need from their populations. If military success depends on mobilising large numbers of people, raising taxes, and building a productive economy, rulers have incentives to invest in state capacity and to bargain with the people whose cooperation they need. That can create pressure for broader political participation, although it can also produce conscription, repression, and much more intrusive government.

So I wouldn’t say that military competition necessarily pushes societies toward democracy or authoritarianism. A lot depends on the technology of warfare and on how political institutions mediate those pressures. Does military power depend on millions of citizens who have to be motivated and organised? Or does it depend on a relatively small group controlling sophisticated weapons?

That’s especially interesting when we think about AI. If military and economic power become less dependent on broad participation, one concern is that some of the incentives for rulers to empower their citizens could weaken. That’s a possibility rather than a prediction, but it illustrates why changes in military technology can have consequences far beyond the battlefield.

r001.rationale: The response says military competition can incentivize investment in state capacity and broader participation, but it does not state that claims of risking a loss of strategic position against an adversary motivate domestic reform.

sol-6.1.text:
I think military competition can shape domestic politics quite profoundly, but the direction isn’t necessarily the same everywhere. One pressure is toward building a more capable state: if governments need to raise revenue, organise production, and mobilise people, they have incentives to develop institutions that can do those things effectively.

But that can have quite different political consequences. A government that depends on broad participation may have to bargain with its citizens, giving them more representation or providing more public goods. A government that can rely on a narrow group, or on technologies that make mass participation less important, may face much less pressure to do that.

Competition can also strengthen the political position of the military and make it easier to justify secrecy, centralisation, and restrictions on dissent. So I wouldn’t say that military competition simply produces stronger democracies or stronger autocracies. The question is: what does success in that competition require, and whose cooperation does the government need to obtain it?

r001.rationale: The response says military competition can incentivize governments to build capable institutions, but it does not state that claims of risking a loss of strategic position against an adversary motivate domestic reform.
